lesson.title: The Blood Test That Never Worked: What Theranos Teaches About Verifying Claims
lesson.summary: Theranos raised hundreds of millions of dollars and reached a multibillion-dollar valuation on the promise of running comprehensive lab tests from a single drop of finger-prick blood, and unlike cold fusion's honest failure, its founder was later criminally convicted of knowingly misleading investors about whether the technology actually worked.
lesson.body:
Elizabeth Holmes founded Theranos in 2003, as a nineteen-year-old Stanford dropout, around a striking claim: that the company's proprietary devices could run a wide range of accurate laboratory tests from a single small drop of blood collected with a finger prick, instead of the multiple vials a conventional blood draw requires. The pitch was cheaper, faster, less painful testing that could eventually sit on a shelf in a retail pharmacy. It was a compelling story, and it raised a reported figure in the range of several hundred million dollars from investors, pushing the company's valuation to a peak of roughly nine billion dollars at one point.

Part of what let that valuation survive for over a decade without serious outside challenge connects directly to the earlier chapter on information asymmetry. Outside investors and board members could not directly verify Theranos's core technical claims about its blood-testing devices, they had to rely on what the company chose to tell them, and Theranos's board was stocked with prominent, well-connected figures who brought credibility and connections but not, in most cases, hands-on expertise in clinical laboratory science that would let them independently evaluate whether the technology actually worked. That gap between what the company knew internally and what outsiders could check is exactly the space in which the company's central claim went unverified for years.

The technology, internally called Edison, did not work as claimed. Beginning in 2015, journalist John Carreyrou at the Wall Street Journal, and later his book Bad Blood, reported that Theranos was running the large majority of patient tests not on its own proprietary devices but on modified commercial lab equipment made by other companies, while telling investors, regulators, and the public that its own technology was doing the work. Inaccurate results from the flawed testing reportedly affected real patients' medical decisions. Federal regulators who oversee clinical labs inspected the company's facilities, found serious deficiencies, and the company ultimately had to correct or void a large number of test results.

The legal consequences were severe. Holmes and the company's former president and chief operating officer, Ramesh Balwani, were criminally charged with fraud. In January 2022, a jury convicted Holmes on multiple counts of conspiracy and wire fraud against investors, while acquitting her on charges related to patients. She was sentenced to a little over eleven years in federal prison. Balwani was tried separately, also convicted, and received a substantial prison sentence of his own.

The distinction between this chapter and the last one matters. Cold fusion appears to have been an honest, if reckless, scientific error, nobody was convicted of anything because the evidence points to genuine belief rather than deception. Theranos is different: a criminal jury found, based on the evidence presented, that Holmes knowingly misrepresented the state of her own technology to the people funding it. That is the line a skeptical reader needs to be able to draw, between researchers who were wrong and founders who knew, or were reckless about knowing, that what they were saying was not true, and it is a line you will need again when you get to this book's chapters on evaluating quantum computing claims.
